title: 2 Kings 2:23–25
context: This short unit should be kept intact and stated as the text gives it, without expanding the violence, without mockery, and without being turned into a joke or a children’s moral. Elisha went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!” He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in the LORD’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of those youths. He went from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria. The WEB’s word, twice, is “youths.” That wording does not by itself settle a precise age. Some readers, and some other translations, hear younger boys, including renderings that use a word such as little; others hear youths or young men, a group large enough to come out of the city and mock a prophet. The taunt is, in this edition, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!” It is plainly mockery; some also hear “Go up” as a jeer tied to Elijah’s having gone up, and some hear only an insult at his appearance. None of those readings should be declared the only sense. The city from which they come is Bethel, a site of northern calf worship in the earlier history of the kings; some therefore read the mockery against the background of hostility to the LORD’s prophet there. The verses themselves say that the youths came out of the city and mocked him; the cultic setting is a suggested background, not a scene this unit spells out. Both traditions report what is written, leave these contested questions as open and hedged options, and do not invent a contrast over prophetic authority.

verses.text: He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!”
verses.arminianNotes:
He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!” The unit begins with a journey toward Bethel and with this mockery on the road. The WEB calls the group “youths.” That English word does not fix their age. Some readers, and some other translations, take them as younger boys, even where a word such as little is used; others take them as youths or young men able to come out as a group. The taunt itself is clear as mockery. Whether “Go up” also jeers at Elijah’s going up, or only insults Elisha’s appearance, is discussed and should not be settled here as fact.

Arminian readers keep the verse inside those limits. They came out of the city, they mocked him, and this is what they said. The line is not to be turned into a joke or a lesson for children.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to add what the sentence does not say, and they refuse to make light of it. The wording is “youths”, and the cry is “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!”

Both traditions state the mockery as it is written and leave the contested questions of age and of the taunt’s full force as hedged options, without a contrast over prophetic authority.

verses.text: He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in the LORD’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of those youths.
verses.arminianNotes:
He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in the LORD’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of those youths. The verse should be reported in that wording, without expanding the violence beyond “mauled” and without inventing a number or a fate the narrator does not add.

Arminian readers let the sequence stand: he sees them, he curses them in the LORD’s name, and two female bears come out of the woods and maul forty-two of those youths. The scene is not to be mocked, softened into a children’s moral, or used to settle the age question already named. Bethel’s earlier idolatry may be offered as background for the city’s hostility, only as a suggested reading, not as a detail this verse states.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same restraint. The curse is in the LORD’s name, and the bears maul forty-two of those youths, as the book says.

Both traditions report the event as the narrator gives it, leave the contested questions hedged, and do not invent a party contrast over the prophet’s authority.

verses.text: He went from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes:
He went from there to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria. The unit ends with a journey, not with further comment on the road at Bethel. Elisha goes to Carmel and then back to Samaria.

Arminian readers hear a plain close. The narrator does not add a moral, an explanation, or a second scene at Bethel. He goes on to Carmel, and from there to Samaria.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the end of the unit and of the chapter’s travel. Mount Carmel and Samaria are named as the next places, nothing more.

Both traditions leave the preceding verses intact behind this close, still without mockery, without a children’s lesson, and without a forced contrast.
